title: Flattering Lips and Flawless Words
summary: David cries for help because faithful people seem to have vanished and everyone around him lies, flatters, and boasts that their tongues make them unstoppable. The LORD answers with a direct promise to rise up for the oppressed. The psalm contrasts the corrupt words of people with the pure words of God, refined like silver, while admitting that the wicked still strut about.
story: Speech has been a thread through the early psalms: slander in Psalm 4, deceitful tongues in Psalm 5, the cursing mouth of the wicked in Psalm 10. Psalm 12 makes it the whole subject. It is a lament not over one enemy but over a whole generation whose words can't be trusted. At its center God himself speaks, the first time in Book 1 since Psalm 2 that a psalm gives the LORD's words directly. The psalm thus contrasts two kinds of speech, human and divine, and sets the reader's hope on the second. Psalm 14 will take up the same picture of a corrupt generation.
historical:
The heading attributes the psalm to David and repeats the musical term Sheminith from Psalm 6. It gives no occasion. Some readers connect it with the intrigues of Saul's court, where informers like Doeg the Edomite (1 Samuel 22) reported David's movements, or with the whispering campaign that preceded Absalom's revolt (2 Samuel 15:1-6), when Absalom won hearts in Israel with smooth words at the city gate. Those are illustrations, not identifications.

Scholars who date the psalm later compare its situation with the prophets' complaints about corrupt societies, such as Micah 7:1-6, where the prophet laments that the godly have perished from the land and that no one can be trusted. The psalm's divine oracle in verse 5 also resembles prophetic speech, and some think a temple prophet or priest spoke that word in answer to the community's lament.
cultural:
In a society where most agreements were oral, trust in someone's word held life together. Contracts, testimony in court, promises between neighbors, and the loyalty of a king's officials all depended on speech. Israel's law forbade false witness (Exodus 20:16) and warned against slander (Leviticus 19:16). The “double heart” of verse 2 is literally a heart and a heart, the Hebrew way of describing someone who says one thing and means another, like merchants who used two sets of weights (Deuteronomy 25:13).

Verse 6 draws on metalworking. Silver was refined by heating ore in a crucible so that impurities separated out. Doing it seven times, the number of completeness in Hebrew thought, describes a perfectly pure product. The “furnace” in the BSB may be a crucible or clay vessel used in the process; the Hebrew here is difficult, and translations vary.
literary: The psalm is a community lament, and it is built in a careful symmetry around its center. Verses 1 and 2 describe the lying generation; verses 3 and 4 pray against their boastful tongues and quote their own arrogant words; verse 5 gives the LORD's answer; verse 6 praises the purity of God's words; and verses 7 and 8 express trust while returning to the present reality of the wicked. The contrast between human speech and divine speech runs throughout: “flattering lips” and “boastful tongue” against “the words of the LORD”. The psalm ends not with a triumphant resolution but with a sober line about vileness being exalted, which keeps the lament honest.

outline.t: Heading and lament: the faithful have vanished
The LORD's answer: I will now arise
The words of the LORD are pure
God keeps his people while the wicked strut about

doctrines.note: Verse 6 says God's words are flawless, refined like silver seven times. Against a culture of lies, God's speech is utterly reliable, and his promises can be trusted.
The psalm shows sin at work in speech: lies, flattery, and the arrogant claim that our words belong to us alone, with no one as our master.
God promises to protect the oppressed and to keep his people from “this generation”. He guards them even while the wicked still move freely.

words.note: Chasid, godly or faithful one. Verse 1 laments that such people are gone. The word describes someone marked by loyal love, the covenant faithfulness God shows and asks of his people. The complaint is not that religion has vanished but that loyalty and trustworthiness have.

Imrah, word or saying. A poetic word used here for the words of the LORD, which are pure (verse 6). It is also a key word in Psalm 119, the great psalm about God's word. The psalm sets God's imrah against the flattering speech of verse 2.

Tsaraph, to refine or smelt. The verb describes a metalworker purifying silver or gold, and it is also used of God testing and purifying his people (Isaiah 48:10; Malachi 3:3). In verse 6 it describes the tested quality of God's word: it has been through the fire and contains no dross.

christ: Psalm 12 contrasts unreliable human speech with the pure word of God. The New Testament presents Jesus as the Word made flesh (John 1:14), full of grace and truth, the one in whom God's speech is perfectly embodied. Jesus also warned that people will give account for every careless word (Matthew 12:36), and James describes the tongue as a fire that can set a whole life ablaze (James 3:6), picking up the psalm's concern. The promise in verse 5 that the LORD will rise up for the oppressed finds its fullest answer in the God who came in Christ to bring good news to the poor. These are thematic connections rather than direct predictions.

hard.q: If God's words are flawless, why does the psalm end with the wicked still in control?
hard.a: Verse 8 is honest: after God's promise and the psalmist's praise, the wicked still wander freely and vileness is still exalted. The psalm does not pretend that the promise has already been fully carried out. It places God's reliable word alongside a world that still looks corrupt, and asks the reader to trust the word more than the appearances. Some interpreters see verse 8 as describing the ongoing situation within which God keeps his people (verse 7); others read it as a final reminder of why the prayer of verse 1 is still needed. Either way, the psalm teaches faith that lives between promise and fulfillment.

questions: Verse 1 laments that faithful people seem to have vanished. Have you ever felt that way, and what helped you see more clearly?
The wicked in verse 4 claim ownership of their words. How do you use speech, including online, as though your words answer to no one?
God's words are compared to silver refined seven times. How does that picture shape the trust you place in Scripture?
